protocols.title: High Voltage Safety
rules: Always disconnect and lock out power before working on electrical components
Verify zero voltage with meter after disconnecting - don't trust the disconnect alone
Discharge all capacitors before touching - they hold lethal charge even after power off
Use insulated tools rated for the voltage you're working with
Never work alone on high-voltage systems - have someone nearby for emergencies
Wet conditions: do NOT work on electrical components - reschedule
Test your meter on a known live source before trusting a 'dead' reading

protocols.title: Refrigerant Safety
rules: EPA Section 608 certification required to purchase and handle refrigerants
Never vent refrigerant to atmosphere - federal violation, $44,539 per day fine
Recover refrigerant into approved DOT cylinders only
Disposable cylinders must NOT be refilled - transport violation
R-32 and R-454B are A2L (mildly flammable) - no open flames, use ventilation
Refrigerant displaces oxygen - never work in enclosed spaces without ventilation
Liquid refrigerant contact causes frostbite - wear gloves and safety glasses
Never use oxygen or compressed air to pressure test - explosion hazard
Use dry nitrogen only for pressure testing (with appropriate regulator)

protocols.title: Rooftop/Ladder Safety
rules: 3-point contact rule on ladders at all times
Ladder angle: 4:1 ratio (1 foot out for every 4 feet up)
Secure ladder at top - tie off or have someone hold
Carry tools in belt or bucket - keep hands free for climbing
On flat roofs: watch for soft spots, skylights, and unmarked openings
Hot roofs in summer: wear appropriate footwear, stay hydrated
Wind above 25 mph: postpone rooftop work
Harness required at heights above 6 feet (OSHA standard)

protocols.title: Gas Line Safety
rules: If you smell gas: evacuate area immediately, do NOT operate any electrical switches
Soap bubble test all gas connections after work
Gas line pressure test: 3 psig for 10 minutes minimum (manometer test)
Verify gas valve off before working on heat exchanger or burners
Check heat exchanger for cracks: visual + carbon monoxide test in supply air
CO level above 9 ppm in supply air = cracked heat exchanger = SHUT DOWN unit
Never bypass safety switches (rollout, high limit, pressure switch)

protocols.title: A2L Refrigerant Safety (R-32, R-454B, R-1234yf)
rules: A2L classification = mildly flammable: lower flammability limit approximately 14% for R-32, 12% for R-454B — requires significant concentration in air to ignite
Burning velocity 10 cm/s or less (R-32: 6.7 cm/s, R-1234yf: 1.5 cm/s) — slow flame propagation, will not detonate
NO open flames, smoking, electrical sparks, or torches within 10 ft of refrigerant work area
Brazing on charged systems is PROHIBITED — always recover refrigerant first, purge with nitrogen during any brazing
Use ONLY A2L-rated tools: recovery machine (UL-listed for A2L), micron gauge with sealed electrical contacts, A2L-rated leak detector, manifold gauges with reverse-flow check valves
Standard halide leak detectors are NOT rated for A2L — illegal and unsafe to use on A2L refrigerants
Ventilation required when working in any enclosed space — mechanical ventilation if natural is insufficient
Do NOT work in below-grade spaces without forced ventilation — A2L refrigerants are heavier than air and accumulate at floor level
A2L equipment has charge limits per room volume per UL 60335-2-40 — smallest serviced room must be adequate for system charge weight
A2L equipment has built-in refrigerant leak detection sensors — DO NOT bypass. Sensor activates indoor blower to disperse any leak below flammable limit.
Recovery cylinders for A2L must be UL-listed specifically for A2L service
Emergency leak response: ventilate immediately, evacuate area, eliminate all ignition sources, do NOT operate any electrical switches in affected area until cleared
Personal protective equipment: safety glasses, cryogenic gloves, avoid synthetic clothing (static spark risk — use natural fibers or arc-rated)
Driver training and DOT requirements for transporting A2L cylinders in service vehicles
Document all A2L service per EPA Section 608 revised requirements including leak repair verification

protocols.title: Confined Space Entry
rules: Confined space definition per OSHA 1910.146: large enough to enter and work, limited means of entry/egress, not designed for continuous occupancy. Includes crawl spaces, attic air handler compartments, mechanical rooms, boiler rooms, equipment vestibules.

Permit-required confined space (PRCS): contains or has potential to contain hazardous atmosphere, engulfment risk, configuration trap, or other recognized serious hazard. Requires written permit, attendant, atmospheric testing, and rescue plan before entry.
Atmospheric testing BEFORE entry in this order: (1) Oxygen 19.5-23.5%, (2) Combustible gases below 10% LEL, (3) Toxic gases — CO below 25 ppm, H2S below 10 ppm
Test atmosphere at multiple depths — top, middle, bottom — heavier-than-air gases (propane, refrigerants) accumulate at bottom; lighter gases (methane) at top
4-gas meter required minimum: O2, LEL, CO, H2S. Calibrated within manufacturer-specified period and bump-tested daily before use.
Continuous atmospheric monitoring during entry — initial test alone is insufficient
Buddy system mandatory: outside attendant must maintain continuous contact (visual, voice, or radio) and must NOT enter to rescue without proper rescue equipment
Rescue plan documented BEFORE entry: who calls 911, who provides retrieval, what retrieval equipment is on-site
Retrieval equipment for vertical entries greater than 5 ft: full-body harness with retrieval line, mechanical retrieval device
Crawl spaces under homes: assess for standing water, sewage gas, rodents, spiders, fiberglass insulation, lead paint, asbestos before entry
Attic air handlers in summer: temperatures 130-160°F or higher — heat stress protocol (sp-007) applies, limit time in space, work early morning when possible
Lockout and tagout all energy sources in confined space BEFORE entry: electrical, refrigerant pressure, gas, mechanical
Know your egress: never enter a space you cannot quickly exit — measure shoulder width against opening
Do NOT enter confined space alone — OSHA standard 1910.146 violation

protocols.title: Heat Stress Prevention
rules: Heat stress risk is highest in: attics (130-160°F or more in summer), rooftop work in direct sun, mechanical rooms, boiler rooms
Pre-hydrate: drink 16 oz water before starting work in any hot environment
During work: drink 8 oz water every 15-20 minutes — small frequent intake, not large amounts at once
Electrolyte replacement on extended hot work: sports drinks, electrolyte tablets, salty snacks
AVOID: alcohol, caffeine, energy drinks — all increase dehydration and heat stress risk
Work-rest ratios per NIOSH guidelines: heat index 90-103°F = 45 min work / 15 min rest per hour; heat index 103-115°F = 30 min work / 30 min rest per hour; above 115°F = postpone non-emergency work
Take rest breaks in shade or air-conditioned area to lower core body temperature
New technicians and those returning after time off require acclimatization — 20% normal workload day 1, increase 20% per day over 7-14 days
Buddy check: monitor coworkers for symptoms, especially during heat waves
HEAT EXHAUSTION symptoms (treatable): heavy sweating, weakness, cool/pale/clammy skin, fast weak pulse, nausea, vomiting, headache, fainting
HEAT EXHAUSTION response: move to cool area, loosen clothing, apply cool wet cloths, sip water, monitor closely, seek medical care if no improvement within 30 minutes
HEAT STROKE symptoms (LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY): high body temperature above 103°F, hot red skin (dry or damp), fast strong pulse, confusion or altered mental status, loss of consciousness, seizure
HEAT STROKE response: CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY, move person to cool place, cool them as fast as possible with cold water or ice packs to neck/armpits/groin, do NOT give fluids to unconscious person
Personal cooling gear: cooling vests with ice packs, cooling neck wraps, lightweight light-colored clothing, wide-brim hat
Schedule heavy work for early morning — peak heat typically 2-5 PM in summer
Rooftop surface temperatures can reach 160-180°F — use kneeling pads, avoid direct skin contact with surfaces
Document any heat-related incidents — employer required to investigate per OSHA general duty clause

protocols.title: Carbon Monoxide Safety
rules: CO is colorless, odorless, tasteless — cannot be detected by human senses. Binds to hemoglobin 200x more readily than oxygen, causing cellular asphyxiation.
All technicians servicing combustion equipment MUST carry calibrated low-level CO detector or combustion analyzer
Personal CO monitor alarm levels: 35 ppm = action level (investigate source), 70 ppm = evacuate area, 200+ ppm = life-threatening, evacuate immediately

INDOOR AIR ACTION LEVELS: 0-9 ppm acceptable background; 9-35 ppm = investigate source immediately; 35-70 ppm = occupants vacate, repair before reoccupying; 70+ ppm = evacuate, call 911 and shut down combustion appliances
FLUE GAS (combustion analyzer in vent pipe): below 100 ppm air-free = acceptable residential furnace; above 400 ppm = service required; above 1000 ppm = shut down appliance
SUPPLY AIR test: ANY measurable CO in supply air above 0 ppm indicates cracked heat exchanger — SHUT DOWN UNIT immediately, do not operate

Heat exchanger crack protocol: (1) verify with multiple methods — visual with scope, CO test in supply air, flame disturbance test with blower on and off; (2) red-tag and shut down; (3) document with photos and CO readings; (4) written notice to customer; (5) do NOT return to service until repaired or replaced

Customer notification for CO hazard must include: equipment ID, CO readings with date/time/location, safety hazard description, recommended action, technician signature, customer acknowledgment signature
CO detectors required on every level and within 10 ft of bedrooms per most residential codes — UL 2034 listed. Replace unit at 7-10 years (sensor degrades).
Combustion analysis required on every furnace tune-up — measure O2, CO, CO2, stack temperature, draft. Document all readings.

Common CO sources to investigate if found in structure: cracked heat exchanger, flue blockage, competing exhaust appliances (clothes dryer, kitchen exhaust, fireplace causing backdraft), gas water heater spillage, attached garage vehicle exhaust

If technician feels symptoms (headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion) during furnace work: EXIT immediately, get fresh air, seek medical care — inform ER of CO exposure for proper blood test (COHb level)
Never operate gasoline-powered equipment (generators, pressure washers) inside or near any building opening
Maintain CO test records on every combustion service call for liability protection and trend analysis

protocols.title: Electrical Arc Flash and Energized Work Safety
rules: Arc flash is an explosive release of electrical energy from a short circuit or phase-to-phase fault. Temperatures reach 35,000°F (4x hotter than sun surface). Pressure waves throw victims, rupture eardrums, and propel molten metal projectiles.
Highest arc flash risk activities: opening energized panels, racking breakers, voltage testing inside live commercial equipment, working near 480V or higher
NFPA 70E governs electrical safety in the workplace — HVAC technicians working in commercial and industrial settings must be familiar with requirements
Always de-energize before working when at all possible — this is the only truly safe condition
If energized work is unavoidable: written energized work permit required per NFPA 70E, documented approach boundaries, qualified electrician only

PPE Categories based on incident energy: CAT 1 (4 cal/cm2) = arc-rated shirt/pants, safety glasses, leather gloves — typical residential 240V work; CAT 2 (8 cal/cm2) = arc-rated coverall, arc flash face shield plus balaclava, hearing protection — typical 480V commercial
Remove all metal jewelry before electrical work: rings, watches, necklaces, metal-frame glasses become conductors and projectiles in arc flash event
Wear only natural fiber (cotton, wool) or arc-rated clothing — synthetic fabrics (nylon, polyester) melt and adhere to skin
Use insulated hand tools rated for system voltage (1000V rated for commercial work)
Test before touch: verify de-energized with CAT III or CAT IV rated meter (for panel and utility-side work)
Test meter on known live source BEFORE and AFTER testing allegedly de-energized circuit
Lockout/tagout: personal lock and tag, key in technician's pocket, only the person who applied the lock removes it
Never share lockout key with another person — each person applies their own lock
Capacitor discharge: motor run capacitors hold lethal charge for several minutes after power off — use 20kΩ 5W resistor with insulated leads to safely discharge before handling
Wet conditions: do NOT perform energized electrical work — postpone or de-energize and wait

Know when to call a licensed electrician: panel modifications beyond simple breaker replacement, service entrance work, conductor sizing changes, any work above 600V, commercial switchgear or MCC work
Working alone on energized equipment is prohibited under NFPA 70E
